title: No Handshake, No Trophy, No Apology: India Face Pakistan in Asian Games Cricket Final
excerpt: The gold-medal match on Saturday in Nagoya carries the sport's fiercest rivalry into the Asian Games — with India's no-handshake stance intact and Mohsin Naqvi staying away from the presentation.
body:
• India and Pakistan face off in the Asian Games men's cricket gold-medal match on Saturday in Nagoya, Japan.
  • India will almost certainly continue its no-handshake stance against Pakistan, in place since the 2025 Asia Cup and backed by a government directive.
  • ACC president Mohsin Naqvi will skip the final, sidestepping a repeat of the Asia Cup trophy-presentation standoffs.
  • India defend the cricket gold they won at Hangzhou 2022; Pakistan are chasing their first men's cricket gold at the Games.

India and Pakistan will contest the Asian Games men's cricket gold medal on Saturday in Nagoya, Japan, after both sides won their semifinals on Thursday. Pakistan beat Bangladesh by six wickets in a match reduced to 13 overs a side because of a wet outfield, while India crushed Sri Lanka by 124 runs. The final sets up another meeting between the sport's fiercest rivals — and once again, the customary handshake is not expected to happen.

The march to the final

Pakistan chased down Bangladesh's 111 for 7 with room to spare. Towhid Hridoy's aggressive 42 off 25 balls, featuring four sixes, gave Bangladesh something to defend, but left-arm spinner Sufyan Muqim's 3 for 28 checked the innings, and Abdul Samad's unbeaten 30 off 15 balls sealed the chase before the 13 overs were up.

India's win was emphatic. Sent in to bat, they posted 169 for 7 on the back of Ishan Kishan's unbeaten 80 off 46 balls, an innings laced with five sixes and four fours. Fifteen-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi announced himself with 38 off the top order, striking two sixes and six fours. Sri Lanka, fielding a second-string lineup, collapsed to 45 all out in 9.5 overs, with Jasprit Bumrah taking two wickets in his opening over and returning figures of 2 for 7. Spinners Axar Patel, Washington Sundar and Abhishek Sharma shared five wickets between them; only Nuwanidu Fernando, with 15, reached double figures.

A rivalry that skips the handshake

The on-field story will share billing with a protocol question that has shadowed India-Pakistan cricket for more than a year. Since the 2025 Asia Cup, Indian teams have refused to shake hands with Pakistani players before or after matches — at the toss or at the game's end. The stance began as a show of solidarity with the victims of the Pahalgam terror attack and with the armed forces personnel involved in Operation Sindoor, and the BCCI has said the position follows a directive from the Government of India.

The policy has hardened across formats. Suryakumar Yadav's side beat Pakistan three times in the Asia Cup, including the final, without shaking hands once and without accepting the trophy from Pakistan Cricket Board chairman Mohsin Naqvi. The women's team followed the same line at the women's Asia Cup in the UAE, declining both the handshakes and the trophy from Naqvi. The approach has carried into Under-19 cricket and into the ongoing Women's ODI World Cup, where captain Harmanpreet Kaur's side also skipped the customary greetings.

It is a cricket-only phenomenon. In other disciplines at these Games, Indian and Pakistani athletes have exchanged the usual handshakes without incident — a contrast that has drawn comment from fans of both countries.

The Naqvi question settles itself

One potential flashpoint has already been defused. Mohsin Naqvi, who is both PCB chairman and president of the Asian Cricket Council, will not attend the gold-medal match. The decision spares the organisers a repeat of the Asia Cup scenes, where India twice left major trophies uncollected rather than accept them from Naqvi. The BCCI had asked for the ACC to let Naqvi's deputy perform the presentation honours; he declined.

At the Asian Games, medals are presented under the authority of the Olympic Council of Asia, not the ACC, so the local organisers can run the ceremony without the PCB chairman on the stage. BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia is expected to be with the Indian contingent in Japan. None of it changes the central contest: the defending champions against a Pakistan side chasing its first men's cricket gold at the Asian Games.

What to watch

For the Indian diaspora — in the United States, the Gulf, and increasingly in Japan itself — this final is appointment viewing. India start as favourites on current form, but Pakistan's chase against Bangladesh showed intent, and finals between these teams rarely follow the script. The cricket begins at 10:00 AM IST on Saturday. Whether the players shake hands at the end of it will say as much about where the rivalry stands off the field as the scoreboard says about where it stands on it.
